title: Counting stamens
teaches: Linnaeus's system of sorting plants by counting stamens, the two-word names that outlived it, how to read a plant's name, and why names and families still change

blocks.text: By the early 1700s European botanists knew several thousand kinds of plant, and had no agreed way to sort them or even to name them. A plant's name was a short Latin description, and a description grew longer as more look-alikes were found. One small ground cherry was *Physalis annua ramosissima, ramis angulosis glabris, foliis dentato-serratis*: the yearly, much-branched physalis, with smooth angled branches and toothed leaves. Two botanists describing the same plant could write different phrases, and a reader could not tell whether they meant the same thing.

In 1735 a 28-year-old Swede, Carl Linnaeus, published *Systema Naturae*, a few large sheets that sorted every plant into one of 24 classes. His method needed only a flower and the ability to count. Look at the stamens (lesson 18's pollen-makers): how many are there, are they separate or fused together, are some longer than others? That gave the class. Then count the styles, the stalks that rise from the flower's central egg-holding parts, the carpels, to get the order within it. Class 24 was for the plants with no flowers to count, the ferns, mosses, seaweeds and fungi.[^lewd]

Students could now place a plant they had never seen in minutes, and they did, all over the world: Linnaeus sent his students on ships to collect, and several died doing it. But Linnaeus knew the classes were artificial. Some held together plants that really are related: his class of four long and two short stamens is the mustard family, and his class of two long and two short is mostly the mints and snapdragons. Others threw together plants with nothing else in common, and split up plants that clearly belonged together.

blocks.text: A family is a group that shares more than one feature: the shape of the flower and fruit, how the leaves are arranged, the chemistry, and, as lesson 21 showed, the DNA. Linnaeus spent the rest of his life collecting fragments of such a natural system, and his successors in France, the Jussieu family, built one by 1789. The stamen counts were dropped within a century.

What lasted was a shortcut. In *Species Plantarum*, in 1753, Linnaeus listed about 6,000 kinds of plant, each with its long descriptive name. In the margin beside each he added a single word, which with the name of the genus made a two-word label for everyday use. The ground cherry became *Physalis angulata*. He meant it as a convenience. It became the rule: every species of living thing now has a two-word name. For plants the count starts in 1753, and a plant name published earlier doesn't count; animal names count from 1758, the edition of *Systema Naturae* where Linnaeus did the same for animals.

The first word is the **genus**, a group of close relatives, written with a capital. The second, the specific name, starts with a lower-case letter, and the two together, in italics, name the **species**: *Quercus garryana*, the Oregon white oak. Genera are grouped into families, whose names end in *-aceae*, built from one of their genera: *Rosaceae*, the rose family, from *Rosa*.

A name often says something about the plant, or its finder. *Quercus garryana* is the oak named for Nicholas Garry of the Hudson's Bay Company. Douglas fir is *Pseudotsuga menziesii*, the false hemlock found by Archibald Menzies, and it is not a true fir at all, which is why careful writers hyphenate it: Douglas-fir. *Camassia quamash*, common camas, is built from *qém'es*, the Nez Perce name for its bulbs. *Angraecum sesquipedale*, the comet orchid, is the orchid a foot and a half long, after its spur. Lesson 18's moth, *Xanthopan praedicta*, is the yellow-all-over one that Darwin predicted.
A name is sometimes followed by an abbreviation, such as *Rosa canina* L. That is the person who first published it; L. is Linnaeus.

Gardeners complain that botanists keep renaming plants. There are two main reasons. First, with a few agreed exceptions, the oldest name wins: if someone finds that a plant was named earlier, by someone else, the earlier name takes over. Second, when DNA shows that a species belongs in a different genus, it moves, taking its specific name with it, and when it shows that a family is really two, the family splits. The lily family has been divided into several, and the snapdragons have moved into the plantain family, which looks nothing like them. Each change is a correction of the record of who is related to whom.
Next time you buy a plant, read its label's Latin name and work out what each word says. Then look up its family.

blocks.caption: Five questions on names and classes
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How did Linnaeus's 1735 system place a plant in a class?
choices: By counting its stamens and noting whether they were joined or of unequal length
By the colour of its petals
By the shape of its leaves
items.why: The class came from the stamens, the order within it from the number of styles. Anyone with a flower could do it.

items.ask: Why was the stamen system dropped?
choices: It grouped some unrelated plants together and split up related ones
Too many plants had the same number of stamens to tell apart
It worked only for European plants
items.why: Linnaeus himself called it artificial. A family is marked by many features shared together, not by one count.

items.ask: In the name *Pseudotsuga menziesii*, what is *Pseudotsuga*?
choices: The name of the person who found it
items.why: The first word of a species' name is its genus, with a capital. The second word here honours Archibald Menzies.

items.ask: A plant is in the family Rosaceae. What can you say about it?
choices: It is in the rose family, named after the genus Rosa
items.why: Family names end in -aceae and are built from one of their genera. Rosaceae includes roses, apples and strawberries.

items.ask: DNA shows that a species belongs in a different genus. What happens to its name?
choices: The genus changes and it keeps its specific name
It keeps both names, one in each genus
It gets a completely new two-word name
items.why: The specific name travels with the species to its new genus, so only the first word changes.

summary: **Linnaeus sorted plants by counting stamens (1735).** The stamens gave the class, the styles the order; anyone could do it.
**The classes were artificial.** Some matched real families, like the mustards; others mixed lilies with barberries.
**A family shares many features at once.** Flower and fruit, leaves, chemistry and, now, DNA.
**Every species has a two-word name, counted from 1753.** Genus with a capital, specific name small, both in italics: *Quercus garryana*.
**Family names end in -aceae.** Rosaceae, the rose family, from *Rosa*.
**Names change for good reasons.** The oldest name wins, and DNA moves species between genera and splits families.

lewd.title: Loathsome harlotry
lewd.text: Linnaeus described stamens and carpels as husbands and wives sharing a bridal bed, and his classes by how many husbands each wife had. The botanist Johann Siegesbeck called it loathsome harlotry, unfit for students. Linnaeus named a small, sticky, unpleasant weed *Sigesbeckia* after him.
